\begin{definition}[Certification system]\label{def:certsys}
A \emph{certification system} consists of a set $S$ of states, a set $I$ of move names, a step
function $\mathrm{step} : S \times I \to S$, a cost $\mathrm{cost} : I \to \mathbb{N}$, and a
reading $\mathrm{cert} : S \to \{\mathrm{no}, \mathrm{yes}\}$, subject to one rule, the
\emph{toll}: for every state $s$ and move $i$,
\[
\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no} \text{ and } \mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s,i)) = \mathrm{yes}
\;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1.
\]
The run of $t = [i_1, \ldots, i_n]$ from $s_0$ ends at $\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$, the result of
applying the steps in order, and its total cost is
$\mathrm{cost}(t) = \mathrm{cost}(i_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{cost}(i_n)$, with the empty run
costing 0.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Entitlement]\label{def:u08-entitlement}
A run is \emph{entitled} to a claim when three things are on hand: an \emph{object} carried in the run's
states; a \emph{checked relation} between that object and the claim, meaning a test that was run
and whose result is on the record; and a \emph{paid event}, a move of the run at which
the object was put in place and which the price list charged at least one. In a certification
system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) a move that takes the reading from no to yes is such a
move, because the toll charges it. This is the book's word; there's no Coq definition of it.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[What the toll prices, and what it doesn't]\label{rem:u09-three}
Read off Definition~\ref{def:certsys} and Observation~\ref{thm:universal-floor}, and checked on the
board as a certification system (\code{nec\_f\_board\_raw\_free}, \code{nec\_f\_board\_floor} and
\code{nec\_f\_board\_floor\_flat}, NecFPaperToys.v). (1) The toll puts no bound on the cost of a raw-observation
move; on Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board STAY and WORK are raw observation and cost $0$. (2) Every certified
insight event is charged at least $1$, by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to
one reading yes has total cost at least $1$, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat:
the floor's proof uses nothing about the end state but its reading, so adding any hypothesis
about what else the end state shows leaves the bound at $1$ and cannot raise it. A system that
wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to write that into its price list, move
by move; the toll doesn't do it for anyone.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Records on reversible machines]\label{thm:u11-reversible}
(1) Let $B$ be a base whose step is injective. The machine with states $(b, r, H, x)$, step
$(b, r, H, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ r :: H,\ x + \delta)$ ($\delta$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}), starting states with $r$ off, $H$ empty and $x = 0$, has an
injective step, and under the supposition of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} it is a base-driven
record over $B$. (2) On a finite state space, a single injective step with a permanent
reading never turns that reading from off to on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Substrate]\label{def:u12-substrate}
A \emph{substrate} has a type of states, a type $\mathrm{Prog}$ of programs, and a run map that
takes a program and a state and either gives back a state or gives nothing. It has a counter
$\mu$ on states and a step relation along which $\mu$ never decreases; an encoding
$\mathrm{enc}$ of programs as states with a decoder $\mathrm{dec}$ such that
$\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(p)) = p$; and a predicate $\mathrm{Rep}$ on maps
$f : \mathrm{Prog} \to \mathrm{Prog}$, the transformations the substrate counts as its own.
Two programs are \emph{equivalent}, $p \simeq q$, when $\mathrm{run}(p, s) = \mathrm{run}(q, s)$
for every state $s$. The last field is the \emph{recursion theorem}: for every $f$ with
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f(p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Halting is undecidable for this machine]\label{thm:u34-undecidable}
The library's two-counter machine agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop, and
its termination match those of the compiled program, so a library problem $(P, a, b)$ halts
if and only if the compiled program halts from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$. Consequently, the
question ``does program $P$ halt from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$?'' is undecidable in the
library's sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape binary Turing machine
halting enumerable.
\end{theorem}

The two-counter machine used by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors agrees with the
INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop, and its termination match those of the compiled program,
so its halting problem at $(P, a, b)$ has a positive answer
if and only if the compiled program halts from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$. Consequently, the
question ``does program $P$ halt from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$?'' is undecidable in the
following reduction sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape binary Turing machine
halting enumerable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The host is Thiele-complete, and $U$'s halting is undecidable]\label{thm:u34-U-complete}
(1) The host machine, with $\mathsf{Slot}$ as its property and one move per instruction, is
Thiele-complete (Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}), and Thiele-complete over its own

floor; a run of $U$ that raises the host's flag costs at least 3 there. The system built from its
Thiele-completeness agrees with it step for step and cost for cost, so the same run costs at least

\begin{definition}[The host]\label{def:u34-host}
A \emph{guest} is a program $P$ of this chapter's machine together with a state $g$ of it
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-step}). A \emph{host state} $h$ has six parts: its own core
$\mathrm{core}(h)$, its ledger $\mu(h)$, its own flag $\mathrm{own}(h)$, the guest program
$P(h)$ held as a list of instructions, the guest state $g(h)$, and the \emph{mirror} $m(h)$, a
yes/no copy of the guest's flag. The host has two kinds of move. $\mathrm{OWN}\ i$ runs the
instruction $i$ on the host's own core, costs what this chapter's machine charges for $i$,
and raises $\mathrm{own}$ exactly when that machine's flag would rise. $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$
costs $b$. If the host's core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to
its next line and, if the guest's next instruction costs at most $b$, runs that instruction
on $g(h)$; in the same move the mirror becomes $m(h) \lor (\lnot\mathrm{cert}(g(h)) \land
\mathrm{cert}(g'))$, where $g'$ is the new guest state. The host's reading is
$\mathrm{own}(h) \lor m(h)$. Its stored program is $U_0 = [\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1;\ \mathrm{OWN}\
(\text{INC } A);\ \mathrm{OWN}\ (\text{DEC } A\ 1)]$: one guest step, then two moves that
bring the host back to its first line. (The Coq file calls it \code{U}; I write $U_0$ here so
nobody mixes it up with the universal program $U$.)
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The compiler is correct]\label{thm:running-compiler}
For every source program with no recursion, and every input: the program computes $y$ exactly when
the runner (the Coq function that gets extracted) halts with $y$ for some amount of fuel; exactly when the compiled host program
halts with $y$; exactly when the two-counter guest halts with $y$; and exactly when $U_P$ running that
guest halts with $y$, with its first counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. So compiling
a program computes its answer and certifies nothing: the compiler is a route to answers, and a
certification has to be written into the source as a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. The runner also
takes exactly as many steps as the host program does, with the rest of its fuel left over, and a run
that doesn't halt has used all its fuel.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}[Sound, and incomplete]\label{rem:u23-sound-not-complete}
The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum question it is usually read against. PSD of
$M(E)$ gives the correlators a PSD completion, since the zeros are one choice of the two free
entries (\code{zero\_marginal\_implies\_elliptope}, ElliptopeCompletion.v). The converse fails.
The all-ones plan has a PSD completion (\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope}), and every
deterministic plan is a quantum strategy (\code{qs\_deterministic\_plan}, QuantumStrategies.v); yet its
minor on rows $A_0, B_0, B_1$ is $1 - 1 - 1 = -1$, so $M(E)$ is not PSD there, and a tally of
one matching round per pair gives $A = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1$ in the integer check, so the check
fails. The second failure is a named theorem on the machine: the tally of one matching round
per pair is refused forever (Proposition~\ref{prop:chsh-demos}). Every deterministic plan fails
the same way. The tally of one round per pair fails the check for each of the sixteen plans
(\code{nec\_e\_check\_refuses\_all\_plans}), so does a plan replayed over any number of rounds once
pairs 00 and 10 have been sampled (\code{nec\_e\_check\_refuses\_deterministic}, NecEChshInt.v), and
no deterministic plan's pinned matrix is PSD (\code{nec\_e\_deterministic\_not\_pinned\_psd},
NecEChsh.v). So a pass proves the bound, and a failure proves only that the tally's pinned matrix isn't
PSD or a pair went unsampled; it says nothing about whether the play was classical or quantum. The free tally from the start of this section is
exactly such a tally: it reaches $S = 2$ and the check throws it out.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[What the name does and does not cover]\label{rem:chsh-fine-scope}
Fine's 1982 theorem is an equivalence between several descriptions of local models and the
Bell inequalities. \code{fine\_theorem} proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys
the bound. Its converse, as it's stated, is false (\code{nec\_e\_fine\_converse\_false}); the
equivalence in the form Fine meant, for correlations, with each correlator between $-1$ and $1$ and all eight inequalities, is
\code{nec\_e\_fine\_iff}. And \code{fine\_theorem} covers only finitely many hidden states
($\lambda \le \lambda_{\max}$). An arbitrary probability space is outside it. The transfer to rational
boxes is \code{local\_box\_CHSH\_bound} (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v): if
\textnormal{\texttt{box\_correlations B}} is factorizable then the real image of $|S(B)|$ is at most 2.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[What PSD of the pinned matrix means]\label{rem:chsh-scope-five}
$M(E)$ is the level-1 moment matrix with the two within-party entries $\langle A_0 A_1
\rangle$ and $\langle B_0 B_1 \rangle$ pinned to zero. Its PSD is sufficient for the
correlators to admit some PSD completion (item G, \code{zero\_marginal\_implies\_elliptope}), and it
is not necessary: the all-ones plan has a completion but fails here. So a check built on
$M(E)$ is sound for the completion set and not complete for it, and it rejects some honest
classical tallies. That correlators with a PSD completion are exactly those reachable by
quantum measurements is Tsirelson's theorem, and both halves are proved here in finite dimension.
For real and for complex amplitudes, a strategy's correlators are inner products of unit vectors
(\code{qs\_corr\_dot}, \code{qs\_uvec\_unit} and \code{qs\_vvec\_unit}; with complex amplitudes,
\code{qc\_corr\_dot}, \code{qc\_uvec\_unit} and \code{qc\_vvec\_unit}, the vectors read as real
ones of twice the length) and its level-1 moment matrix is PSD (\code{qs\_npa\_psd},
\code{qc\_npa\_psd}), so they have a PSD completion (\code{tr\_quantum\_elliptope},
\code{tr\_complex\_elliptope}). The other half, that every PSD completion comes from a quantum
strategy, is \code{tr\_representation}: the strategy is built on two eight-level systems from
the completion's Gram vectors (item H).
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Fraction-free Schur step]\label{lem:chsh-schur-step}
For a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $h$ and any vector $v$, with
$S_{ij} = h_{11} h_{ij} - h_{1i} h_{1j}$ for $i, j \ge 2$ (here $S$ is the Schur matrix;
the score plays no part
in this lemma),
\[
h_{11} \, v^{\mathsf T} h\, v = \Bigl(\sum_{j} h_{1j} v_j\Bigr)^2 + \sum_{i,j \ge 2} S_{ij} v_i v_j .
\]
So if $h_{11} > 0$ and the $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ matrix $S$ gives a nonnegative form, then $h$
does too. The instances used are \code{sym6\_Schur\_identity} (QuantumPartitionPSD\_\allowbreak{}1AB.v) and
\code{sym5\_Schur\_identity}, with the conclusions \code{sym6\_qf\_nonneg\_from\_pd} and
\code{sym5\_qf\_nonneg\_from\_pd}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{remark}[Interior only]\label{rem:chsh-interior}
Every test in the cascade is strict, so a passing check certifies that $H$ is positive
definite, which is stronger than semidefinite. A point where $H$ is PSD but singular cannot pass, and
neither can a moment with $|\gamma_k| = 1$. For example, the tally of item E with correlators
$(3/5, 4/5, 4/5, -3/5)$ has $H_{11} = 1 - 9/25 - 16/25 = 0$, so the full 1+AB check fails on it
for every choice of $\gamma$, though the level-1 check of item E accepts it
(\code{nec\_e\_singular\_full\_fails} and \code{nec\_e\_singular\_level1\_passes},
NecEChshEquality.v). The source proves
soundness only; no converse is stated.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Convexity and finite mixtures]\label{thm:chsh-ell-convex}
For $0 \le \lambda \le 1$, if $E$ and $F$ are elliptope realizable, so is
$\lambda E + (1 - \lambda) F$ (\code{elliptope\_convex}, ElliptopeCompletion.v). For finitely
many members with nonnegative weights summing to at most 1, the weighted sum is realizable
(\code{elliptope\_finite\_mixture}). Every finite mixture of deterministic plans is realizable
(\code{lhv\_mixture\_elliptope}).
\end{theorem}
